item.title: Taking retroactive grants from concept to practice at Gitcoin Grants Round 11
item.dc:creator: OpenGSN
item.content:encoded:
The OpenGSN team is proud to announce:

  • We’re booting up our Ecosystem support program with Vitalik as policymaker, Yoav Weiss and Austin Griffith as domain experts.
  • Having experienced the challenges with traditional grant funding first hand, we are eager to help take retroactive grants from concept to practice as soon as possible.
  • To get the ball rolling, we are committing $50K to the first experiment with retroactive grants funding as part of a side round in Gitcoin Grants Round 11.
  • Moving forward the idea is to focus on retroactive grants for funding the most underrated public goods in areas where we believe we can exercise good judgement: tooling for retroactive grants, dev tooling & decentralized infrastructure.
  • We hope this will be the first of many experiments in retroactive grants funding for public goods. Big things have small beginnings. We are hoping what we end up learning helps other teams, most notably our friends from Optimism, hit the ground running with their own retroactive grant programs
  • This will be the first deployment of funding since we announced the launch of GSN governance with 5% of tokens allocated to supporting Ethereum public goods, because:
“As Vitalik suggested in his post on legitimacy, it will be healthier and more sustainable for the Ethereum ecosystem if part of the way projects compete for legitimacy is by trying to outdo each other in running the most prestigious ecosystem support programs. If we could establish this as part of the Ethereum culture that will bring a lot more decentralized resources, attention and diversity to the development of public goods. We’re committed to helping get this to work and are looking forward to doing our part to support the wider ecosystem“

Retroactive grants as ecosystem fertilizer

It’s hard to compare the public goods ecosystem we have today with the ecosystem we could have had under a better public goods funding model. We can’t see the projects that were never seeded or the seeds that never took root, but we can consider whether conditions in which we expect things to grow are closer to a metaphorical desert or rainforest.

Today, getting the support to create a public good is arguably harder than getting funded by VCs to build a private good of similar complexity. Who you know can matter more than what you know. Outside an exclusive club of known contributors working on known projects, getting funded can be more difficult than doing the actual work and the difficulty increases exponentially with the amount required. Getting approved for $250K is not 10 times harder than getting approved for $25K, it’s closer to 100 times harder.

If you’re brave enough to try you may find yourself in a catch-22 paradox. To get funded you need credibility, to get credibility you need to do the work, but to do the work you need to get funded. What if you decide to cut through this Gordian Knot and burn through your savings to do the work? Well, thanks to a common but misguided policy of “no funding for past work” you won’t get your savings back, and you’ll also get less recognition because the grant giving organizations won’t promote you as a grantee since they didn’t fund you.

Penalizing permission-less innovation this way makes no sense. If we want a thousand flowers to bloom, we can’t spray our fields with herbicide.

In a sane world, we would be seeking out these heros for taking initiative and serving the public good with no guarantee that it would work out. We would make examples of them to inspire more of our best and brightest to do the same without slowing down to ask for permission. We’d lavish them with fame and fortune. We’d honor them at the Crypto Oscars for an outstanding performance. We’d reward them financially in proportion to the value created and the risk assumed. The best teams building public goods will be able to raise from private investors just like teams building private goods.

Where to start? Setting an example

Having a big vision for a better future is great, but to get the ball rolling we need empirical examples of things working out that we can start pointing to. The more examples we have the realer this gets for those that want to contribute but are hesitating because they’re not sure it’ll work out for them.

We can start by setting up simple retroactive grants programs that make examples of existing public good projects. The sooner we start, the sooner we start learning from experience and start validating which theoretical principles work in practice. This could come in handy when we are ready to start scaling retroactive grants with public good tokens and clever mechanism designs built around them.

A retroactive grants program so simple it might actually work

The basic ingredients:

  • A source of public goods funding
  • A policymaker for high-level guidance and supervision
  • A domain expert for curation
  • A Gitcoin Grants Round for signal boosting
  • Grantee gets financial support, recognition, and trophy NFTs signed by all involved

A source of funding partners with a policymaker, a person trusted by the community to have good judgement and good intentions. The policymaker sets high level guidance and supervision. This guidance can start out with something very simple like: hey, let’s support the most underrated public goods in areas where we have enough domain expertise to evaluate the work.

The domain expert is recruited by the policymaker. This person may not be as well known in the community but is trusted by the policymaker. The expert’s job is to discover good work and apply judgement to come up with a list of retroactive grants.

A portion of the grant funding is allocated on Gitcoin using QF. Getting the community involved helps amplify the recognition grantees receive while also providing additional funding.

At the end of the Gitcoin round NFTs are minted commemorating each grant, symbolically signed by everyone who helped make the grant happen, including the policymaker, domain expert and Gitcoin community members.

In the future, these NFTs will be showcased in various public goods halls of fame.

Join us on Discord: https://discord.gg/NXXTCbh58s

Links

  • Retroactive Public Goods Funding @ Optimism blog
  • Vitalik’s talk on things that matter outside of Defi

Taking retroactive grants from concept to practice at Gitcoin Grants Round 11 was originally published in OpenGSN on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Decentralization is 10X harder. Is it really worth it?
item.dc:creator: OpenGSN
item.content:encoded:
Developing GSN as a decentralized system was much harder than developing a more centralized gas abstraction solution that provided the same functionality. We estimate that could be done with about 10% of the time and effort it’s taken to develop GSN. You could say we’ve been doing things the hard way.

This isn’t just true for GSN. We’ve come to realize that any problem with decentralized systems can be easily “solved” with a solution that is simple, cheap and centralized. This sounds obvious but it can actually be quite tricky because there are many subtle yet important ways in which a solution can be centralized.

This is similar to how there are many non-obvious ways a rocket can be critically flawed. To a non rocket scientist, it can be hard to predict which rocket is going to the moon and which will explode on the way. You could try asking the rocket scientists, but if you don’t know who they are, it can be hard to tell who’s the real deal and who’s just good at pretending on the Internet.

It’s not a perfect metaphor, because while both decentralized systems and rockets are occasionally sold as vehicles for getting to the moon, the more abstract destination of decentralization can be a bit harder to understand.

This can be a problem because if we don’t understand where we are going and what type of solutions can get us there, we’ll be tempted to support “fixing” problems with decentralized systems in ways that trade off what makes them interesting in the first place. Without understanding, it’s not even guaranteed everyone will be able to spot obvious fakes, like a “moon rocket” made of cheap plastic or a “decentralized blockchain” that can somehow coordinate an emergency network upgrade in 2 hours. Without understanding, we risk having to wait until something explodes.

So let’s start with where we’re trying to get to. Why does it make sense to put in 10X the effort to solve some relatively easy problem “the harder more decentralized way”?

What’s so bad about centralization anyway?

Society advances by increasing the number of things we can achieve without having to think about them. When you trust something you don’t have to think about it. You trust the light to turn on when you flick the switch and indeed somehow, magically it does! If this sort of thing goes on for long enough, stuff recedes into the background so much we forget what it’s called.

The most trustworthy systems are the ones that rely the least on human infallibility. This is especially true for systems that aim to solve global coordination problems. The more they scale, the more power flows through them, the greater the prize for exploiting their weaknesses. In this kind of situation, the less we have to rely on the incorruptibility of our systems, the more trust we can squeeze out of them, the more we can take them for granted and just get on with our lives. Unfortunately, the security of centralized systems, like many of our human institutions, doesn’t scale well because they concentrate too much power in the hands of too few.

This can be a fragile arrangement. People get carried away. By greed and fear. By politics. Wanting to be liked. Finding religion. Joining a movement. Jockeying for position. Pandering to supporters. Following trends. Copying each other’s fashions. Huddling for safety. Caring more about who is friend or foe than what is good or bad. Is it left or right or wrong and right? Or maybe vice versa? We’re emotional, irrational and deeply tribal creatures, capable of almost anything, even genocide. We sleepwalk through life, hypnotized by our egos, dwelling more on the petty differences that divide us than our shared condition. 2.5 millions years after emerging from the African savannah, we are still mostly future shocked apes better equipped to rationalize than reason.

So it’s better to design systems around the assumption that we’re all fallible.

Decentralized technology to the rescue!

Decentralized automation that can operate at global scale predictably and transparently can be part of the solution. Whereas the future state of our institutions depends on politics, customs and laws that can all change unpredictably, the future state of decentralized systems can be made to rely more on the predictable laws of physics.

It’s important to distinguish between centralized and decentralized technologies, because centralized technologies tend to amplify the power of centralized institutions we currently have to trust, for good and bad, while decentralized technologies may reduce the need to trust them in the first place.

Decentralized systems are also powerful because they rely on opt-in participation and consent. Perhaps it’s true that up until recently, the only way we could coordinate society at scale was to institutionalize the power of people with guns to force everyone to follow the rules. If this really is the only way to have civilization, we have to rationalize this state of affairs as the lesser evil.

But now it seems like we’ve figured out ways to solve coordination problems at scale without violence. Different decentralized systems of rules can compete globally for legitimacy instead of military supremacy. Wouldn’t it be nice to have more of that?

To make a long story short

Decentralization matters because we are fallible creatures. We need healthy checks and balances so mistakes get corrected. We need more peaceful ways to solve global problems. We need more safe ways to automate mundane things away so we can focus more on what really matters and climb up our ladders of potential.

The benefits of decentralization may seem abstract sometimes, but having more of it in the right places will one day make a big concrete difference. If we play our cards right, we’ll end with global systems that work so well we can take them for granted and just forget about them (until we go camping off world. To the moon!)

Decentralization is 10X harder. Is it really worth it? was originally published in OpenGSN on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: What’s technically new in GSN v2?
item.dc:creator: OpenGSN
item.content:encoded:
This post focuses on the technical changes in GSN v2. For a more general overview see GSN v2 launched as a community governed public good.

We’ve improved GSN v2 with everything we’ve learned since launching GSN v1 to mainnet in August 2019.

Improved architecture — modular & composable

GSN v1 had several issues but one of the most fundamental was that it was a big monolithic system with an all or nothing design, implemented as one giant contract. The basic principles were documented in 1–800-Ethereum & EIP 1613, but there were a lot of subtle details. When we talked to developers we realized they felt like they had to understand and trust all of it before they could use any of it. That added friction.

The new modular architecture of GSN v2 fixes that:

  • Minimum viable trust: instead of needing to trust a big contract that does it all, dapps only have to trust a minimal forwarding contract.
  • Minimum viable contract modification: Only a small modification is required for a contract to support EIP 2771 and receive GSN transactions natively. All that’s needed is inheriting from base class and replacing msg.sender with _msgSender():
  • Architectural support for already deployed mainnet contracts: deploying a tiny per-user proxy that supports EIP 2771 makes it possible to interact with unmodified contracts (e.g., legacy ERC20 tokens). This additional step can be done seamlessly by a wallet or dapp. It costs extra but only needs to be performed once per user, after which the user can interact through GSN with any unmodified contract.
  • Minimum viable understanding: thanks to a new preferred relay mechanism that supports at-cost routing of transactions, the best practice is for each dapp to set up its own relay servers. This frees developers from needing to understand & trust the GSN’s fancy mechanism design. There’s still a decentralized “one for all and all for one” relay server registry, but a dapp only falls back to that if its own relay servers can’t be reached. This happens automatically in a way that prioritizes third party relay servers with competitive transaction fees.
  • Secure plug & play gas payment logic: developers no longer need to bundle complex gas payment logic with every contract that receives meta transactions, which makes integration more difficult and could also potentially open up security vulnerabilities. Instead, gas payment logic now lives in a separate contract that implements the Paymaster interface. This also improves composability as paymasters can be shared between dapps, and one dapp can plug into multiple paymasters. This allows an ecosystem of paymasters to be developed in the future.

Improved “one for all, all for one” security model

The way GSN v2 works, if Alice routes her dapp through her own relays she avoids the transaction fee third party relay servers would charge. However, if Alice’s relay servers are attacked (e.g DDoS) GSN will route her users automatically through Bob’s third party relay servers that charge a competitive rate. Thanks to the smart contract that connects them, Alice doesn’t need to know or trust Bob and vice versa. It’s a decentralized one for all and all for one scheme that ensures that censoring Alice’s users is as hard as censoring all dapps using GSN. The more dapps participate in GSN the more robust the availability guarantee.

Improved gas griefing mitigations

Nobody wants to pay gas for unwanted transactions. GSN v2 minimizes the vulnerability of both dapps and relay servers to gas griefing attacks with multiple protocol level mitigations that are turned on by default. It also provides a set of tools that allows participants to set risk tolerances, choose between trade offs and customize mitigations to match their use case.

Paymasters can implement arbitrary logic for preventing the payment of gas fees for unwanted transactions. For example, a paymaster can require anonymous users to calculate hashcash, or use an external’s service to verify the user solved a captcha, or require users to authenticate via OAuth, or to provide a credit card, etc.

We’re developing reference Paymasters that can be used as-is or as a starting point for further development.

Improved wallet support

Fixing bad & insecure wallet UX with EIP 712: In GSN v1, users of dapps were asked to sign an opaque hash of their transaction without being able to review the contents of the transaction they were supposedly authorizing. This made it impossible to provide informed consent, which was a serious problem from both a security and UX standpoint.

To mitigate this problem GSN v2 now encodes transactions in EIP 712, a structured message format that is widely supported by wallets. This allows the wallet to display the contents of a transaction before the user signs it, just like a regular transaction. A rough example:

Supporting Wallet Connect: we also made it easier to integrate GSN-enabled dapps with mobile wallets by adding support for Wallet Connect. This standard allows mobile wallets to sign transactions that are created by a browser running on another computer that is not given access to the user’s private keys.

Minimal viable governance: derived from Uniswap governance contracts, with minimal changes to make the contracts GSN compatible so they’re capable of abstracting away gas for governance participants. To make it easier for the community to participate in governance we also halved the initial minimal threshold for proposal creation from 1% to 0.5% and the voting quorom from 4% to %2. The only other change makes vesting contracts more configurable, optionally allowing delegation and setting up a transfer pre-approval that allows vesting to be cancelled by governance. For more details, see GSN v2 launched as a community governed public good.

Improved standardization with EIP 2771

With the help of our EIP 2771 co-authors we defined a contract interface standard for receiving meta transactions that could be broadly supported by the community. Thanks guys!

Improved public services

Public service paymasters (on testnets)

Another public service we maintain are “pay for everything” paymasters on testnets that developers can leverage to rapidly prototype demo dapps that work without gas. Users will be able try out demos of dapps that leverage our paymasters without first obtaining testnet tokens from faucets.

Public service relay servers

To make it easier for developers to get started quickly we are running public service relay servers on each network we support.

To avoid our servers becoming the default central points of failure, we charge a ridiculously expensive 70% transaction fee. This means our relays will be the last resort, since the GSN JavaScript client is programmed to prioritize relay servers by cost. To minimize costs and make the network more decentralized we encourage everyone not to rely on our relays and instead run their own.

What’s going to happen to GSN v1?

We consider GSN v1 to be deprecated but the beauty of a decentralized system is that it is not under anyone’s control. Not even its creators!

What’s technically new in GSN v2? was originally published in OpenGSN on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: GSN v2 launched as a community governed public good
item.dc:creator: OpenGSN
item.content:encoded:
Special thanks to Vitalik Buterin and Aya Miyaguchi for ideas, feedback and review.

After a year and a half of development and two security audits the OpenGSN team is proud to announce that v2 of GSN, the Ethereum Gas Station Network, has been launched as a community governed public good. It is ready for production on Ethereum, Polygon Matic, Ethereum Classic and the xDAI networks.

Stats: airdrop to 92,425 early users, 15 design partners, answers to 500+ questions by 343 developers on our Telegram support channel and forum, 11 beta versions, 19 repos, 292+ pull requests.

Development of GSN v2 as an open source public good was sponsored by grants from the Ethereum Foundation, Ethereum Classic and MakerDAO.

Many thanks also to Reddit, OpenZeppelin, Augur, ENS, Infura, Gnosis, Loopring, PoolTogether, Portis and many others for using GSN, making meaningful contributions, providing vital feedback and for allowing use of their brand on the new OpenGSN website. Having good design partners puts the wind in our sails and helps us make sure we were solving the most important problems.

Special thanks to ETHGlobal, whose excellent hackathons last year provided an enthusiastic audience of dapp developers who tested beta versions and gave us amazing feedback on the ease of integration and quality of the new documentation. Extra special thanks to OpenZeppelin for pro-bono research that uncovered a transaction malleability last year before our audits.

Governance TLDR

  • Initial airdrop distributed 10% of the community pool
  • 90% of all pool allocations are locked, released over 4 years
  • 0% VCs / private investors

See GSN community governance for more details.

Contracts

  • GSN.opengsn.eth:
    0xd4b5f1C12B46447693Ae5ec05880fFd117277D12
  • governance.opengsn.eth: 0xe2ed5585dCA01D068f1520eb50fa0C79fa38D0Eb
  • timelock.opengsn.eth: 0x05319d82fa69EA8434A967CdF4A2699Db4Ff40e8

Technical TLDR

GSN v2 improves on GSN v1 by breaking apart its monolithic architecture into a composable, extendible system that:

  1. Improves security on multiple levels
  2. Dramatically simplifies dapp integration
  3. Improves incentives for running relay servers
  4. Supports more flexible gas reimbursement policies
  5. Supports light proxies for interacting with unmodified mainnet contracts
  6. Improves wallet UX by supporting Wallet Connect and EIP 712 encoding
  7. Standardizes the interface for meta transaction recipients with EIP 2771

See What’s technically new in GSN v2 for more details.

Who the hell needs GSN?

Karish (not his real name) is a young Ethereum developer from a country ravaged by years of civil war. We met in 2019. He was sponsored to come to Devcon Osaka as an EF scholar. Given where he comes from it took several minor miracles and months of work to figure out how to fly him to Japan. We sat next to him at a dinner event and ended up talking. His story highlights the usability issues with Ethereum that we can now fix with GSN.

Where Karish lives, the only semi-reliable way to access the Internet is to get a data SIM prepaid in cash. He taught himself English and then programming. There was limited development work in his country so he had to look for work online. The hardest challenge wasn’t doing the development work he loved, it was just getting paid.

Karish doesn’t have a bank account. He doesn’t have papers so he can’t meet the “standard” KYC requirements, which means he’s locked out of centralized services like PayPal and most freelancing platforms. Like two billion other people around the world his only crime was being born in the wrong place.

Karish didn’t let that stop him. He kept looking until he found a job at a small European firm run by a former refugee. They agreed to take a chance on him and to pay his modest wages in ETH. They couldn’t pay him that well but after months of searching he was grateful to get anything. The extra money could help his family. The tricky part was that before he could spend any of it, he would have to find a local who would exchange ETH for cash.

Unlucky for Karish, it took him months to find anyone and the price crashed first. It kept going down and down while he was hoping it would recover. By the time he swallowed the loss and used a DEX to convert to DAI he lost 50% of his hard-earned wages. He promised himself not to speculate in the future and make it a habit to convert his earnings to DAI, leaving a minimal amount of ETH for gas.

When Karish finally meets Gasan, a local buyer willing to exchange crypto for cash, it turns out he only accepts Bitcoin. Karish tries to convince Gasan to accept DAI and offers to help teach him how Ethereum works. They open an Ethereum wallet together to which Karish sends 1 DAI.

Karish shows Gasan how to look up a transaction on etherscan. Gasan explores and clicks through to Karish’s address, where he can see Karish’s entire transaction history. “Why are you only using one address?”

Karish explains that in theory most Ethereum wallets will let you create as many addresses as you want, but it can be a major hassle to split your tokens between addresses for privacy because you’ll still need to maintain a separate ETH balance for each address in order to pay for gas. If any of your addresses runs out of ETH you won’t be able to send it more ETH from another address without linking both addresses to the same owner.

“Wait”, Gasan asks. “So I can’t send the DAI back to your wallet unless you also send me some ETH first to pay the transaction fee?”. “Yes”, Karish answers. How much ETH? Well, that depends on the gas price. Who determines the price? Nobody does, it’s a decentralized auction for block space.

“So what’s the point of holding these tokens if I won’t have privacy and I’ll still need an unpredictable amount of ETH in the same address to do anything with them in the future?”.

Karish explains all the ways tokens can be special thanks to the power of smart contracts. He gives as an example how decentralized contracts peg the value of DAI to USD. It’s a little too much for Gasan to absorb in one sitting so he decides for now he’s only willing to accept ETH. Karish tries converting his DAI back to ETH, but ends up setting the gas price too low. The transaction gets stuck. They agree to meet up later.

With the new version of GSN, Karish’s transaction wouldn’t get stuck because the relay server would automatically bump up the gas fee to adjust for congestion.

He would be able to pay for gas in any token without being at the mercy of a centralized service that could block him.

It’d be easier for him to maintain his privacy by splitting his token activity between as many addresses as he wants. He could even use a new generation of wallets optimized for privacy by default. His wallet could automatically generate a new address for every transaction. For even more privacy, he could send funds into a ZK mixer, and later pull them out without needing tainted ETH for withdrawal.

It would also be easier for Karish to get Gasan excited about all the special things he can do with Ethereum. He wouldn’t need to explain too many new concepts.

Using GSN to abstract away gas means dapps can be a lot more like webapps. They can hide UX complexities that would otherwise confuse many new users and block mass adoption. With the magic of counterfactual contracts, a viral dapp with the simplicity of PayPal could send private payments by email to users that haven’t even created a wallet yet! All without ever compromising on the decentralization that makes it possible to include Karish and billions like him in the opportunities of the global economy.

GSN in a nutshell

GSN is an open source public good that helps dapps reduce UX friction by abstracting away gas. Behind the scenes, GSN provides a decentralized infrastructure that allows dapps to interact with smart contracts even when users don’t have ETH to pay for gas.

Before GSN, it was only possible to achieve this by trusting a centralized third party. GSN on the other hand, is designed like the blockchain itself from the bottom up as a decentralized, permissionless system that does not rely on trusted third parties. This helps dapp developers create user experiences that abstract away gas to more closely resemble the Web 2 UX that users are already familiar with. Without compromising on the decentralization and security that makes Ethereum interesting in the first place.

Examples use cases:

  • More seamless decentralized onboarding of new users to dapps of all kinds
  • Paying for gas in ERC20 tokens (e.g., DAI, BUSD)
  • Paying transaction fees in fiat (e.g., with a credit card)
  • ETH-less withdrawals from stealth addresses (e.g., Umbra) and mixers
  • ETH-less deployment of smart contract wallets at counterfactual addresses

GSN community governance

The need for decentralized governance

As Ethereum evolves, GSN needs to evolve with it. This will be necessary at a minimum to keep up with the network upgrades (e.g., the recent Penalizer security update required by Berlin’s EIP-2930), though we’re optimistic we can do more than that with the community’s support.

This will require aligning incentives, innovation and hard work. It will also require making choices, sometimes hard choices, between trade offs. That requires governance and if there’s going to be governance it can’t be centralized. The founding team will play an important role initially, but its importance relative to the community will shrink as GSN grows.

What does governance control?

Community programs: GSN works better with strong network effects. These can be catalyzed with programs that distribute governance in proportion to participation. The airdrop was the first step. Future programs will be under the control of governance.

Cancellation of vesting: GSN vesting contracts can be set up to allow governance to cancel them by withdrawing the unvested portion. The team vesting contract is set up this way. We believe this improves incentives alignment. Otherwise whatever the contract is called it’s not really “vesting” but a contract that merely delays the distributions of tokens, even when someone leaves.

RelayHub configuration: governance controls economic security parameters such as the minimum stake size, which needs to be proportional to risk. As the volume of transactions grows, such security parameters may need to be adjusted, to maintain the health of the network (either to lower costs or deter fraud).

RelayHub depreciation: governance can set a block number after which an old instance of RelayHub will no longer accept transactions. This is used to protect users from security issues such as breaking changes in Ethereum network upgrades. For example, we delayed the release to fix an issue introduced by Berlin that weakened how GSN handles fraud-proofs. Hopefully breaking changes become less common, but it’s doubtful they won’t happen at all.

Minor changes, such as adjustments to gas costs, can be handled by a change to the RelayHub configuration, so deploying a new version of the contract and depreciating the old one will not be required.

Upcoming version registry: an on-chain registry of canonical contracts, server software and client library versions. Using it will be optional. This will make it easier for GSN participants to stay up to date with the latest, most secure versions of all components.

The GSN governance contracts live exclusively on the Ethereum mainnet. To control contracts on other chains from Ethereum a signalling mechanism is used. Initially, execution of governance’s decisions on non-Ethereum chains will be delegated to the team, relying on their incentives alignment as significant stakeholders in governance. Later, control over non-Ethereum contracts will be transferred to a fully decentralized bridge mechanism. Several cross-chain bridge solutions are currently being evaluated.

Governance parameters:

  • 0.5% of votes are required to create a proposal
  • 2% minimum quorum for a proposal to pass
  • 7 day voting period
  • 2 day timelock on accepted proposals

Allocation pools — 90% released over 4 years

Community: 60% (600,000,000) of token supply. Out of that, 10% (60,000,000) have already been airdropped to the addresses of 92,425 GSN participants. The remaining 90% (540,000,000) will be released to governance over the next 4 years, according to a contract-enforced schedule. More details on the airdrop and future community allocations in the next section of this post.

Team: 19.5% (195,500,000) of token supply. 10% (19,500,000) released immediately to a multi-sig controlled by current and future team members. 90% (17,550,000) in a 4-year vesting contract that can be cancelled by governance. Until the community holds the majority voting power, this pool will abstain from voting except as a last resort to protect protocol security.

Sponsors: 14.5% (145,000,000) of token supply. 10% (14,500,000) released immediately, 90% (130,500,000) locked within 4-year vesting contracts. Sponsors provided non-profit grants to develop GSN as an open source public good. They include the Ethereum Foundation, MakerDAO, ETC Labs, Binance X and unpaid GSN team members who provided “grants” of their time.

Ecosystem supporters program: 5% (50,000,000) of token supply. 10% (5,000,000) released immediately for allocation to supporters of public goods in the Ethereum ecosystem (e.g., client teams, key developer tools). The remaining 90% (45,000,000) will be distributed over the next 4 years, according to a contract-enforced release schedule. The initial setup allows allocations to be managed by the team (with full transparency), but this de-facto delegation is expected to be changed by governance as the program scales.

Philanthropic voices program: 1% (10,000,000) of token supply. 10% (1,000,000) released immediately for allocation to the supporters of charitable projects around the world. The remaining 90% vested. The technical setup is the same as with the ecosystem supporters program but pledged to a different class of recipients.

We are hoping giving altruistic voices a symbolic stake in governance will help feed our sense of purpose as a community, inspire us to keep the big picture in mind, and commit us to supporting things that are not only good for GSN and Ethereum, but also good within the context of the increasingly interconnected world we’re all a part of.

VCs / private investors: 0% of token supply. 100% of the funding to develop GSN has come from non-profit grants.

Airdrop

10% (60,000,000 tokens) of the community pool has been allocated to GSN participants on 5 chains. This includes 92,134 early users (400 each), 211 developers (30,000 each) and 52 relay operators (30,000 each).

These tokens can be claimed immediately with no restrictions on voting or transferability. The redemption period is 1 year. Tokens that have not been claimed in the next 12 months will be swept back into the community pool.

The rest of the airdrop allocation was divided between 15 integration partners and 13 community advisors under the same terms as the development team: 90% locked in 4-year vesting contracts that can participate in governance. The vesting period begins June 20th 2021 and ends April 20th 2025.

To claim your airdropped tokens go to governance.opengsn.org. A popup will show up if your address was included in the airdrop:

For more details check out the airdrop source code: github.com/opengsn/gsn-airdrop

Community pool

The initial airdrop distributed 10% (60,000,000) of the community pool to past GSN participants that were active in the last 2 years. The remaining 90% (540,000,000) of the supply will be distributed to active participants over the next 4 years according to the following schedule:

  • Year 1: 40% (216,000,000)
  • Year 2: 30% (162,000,000)
  • Year 3: 20% (108,000,000)
  • Year 4: 10% (54,000,000)

We expect these distributions to include a range of participation mining programs, community development grants, governance decentralization initiatives and other proposals approved by governance.

A monthly release schedule to the governance treasury is implemented on-chain by 4 immutable vesting contracts. A transfer approval has been pre-configured with the governance treasury as the sole beneficiary for the vesting contract implementing the release schedule for the first 12 months.

Why 5% to an “ecosystem supporters program”?

As Vitalik suggested in his post on legitimacy, it will be healthier and more sustainable for the Ethereum ecosystem if part of the way projects compete for legitimacy is by trying to outdo each other in running the most prestigious ecosystem support programs.

If we could establish this as part of the Ethereum culture that will bring a lot more decentralized resources, attention and diversity to the development of public goods. We’re committed to helping get this to work and are looking forward to doing our part to support the wider ecosystem that supports GSN. We encourage other projects that are on the fence about this to do the same.

We can’t just rely on the Ethereum Foundation for our public goods

The EF is the Ethereum community’s giving tree. It is being gradually cut down to provide more resources for public goods than all other sources combined.

Anyone that has tried working with the EF on a public good knows the grant funding process isn’t perfect. The GSN team has worked closely with the EF in the last couple of years and we’ve come to understand and appreciate how challenging EF’s role is.

They are the non-profit caretaker of a forest where money is sometimes literally growing on trees. It’s insanely hard to find the kind of people who can tend to that without going crazy with jealousy and greed.

“Hey there talented person, can we interest you in a job in an exciting new space? Oh sorry, it’s for a non-profit so we can’t pay well, but you’ll have the satisfaction of knowing that if we’re successful a lot of people that benefit from our work could end up making a lot of money.
Say what, forever in our debt? No no, they won’t be especially grateful. To be honest, we try not to take credit so they probably won’t even notice. We mostly get complaints and have to keep smiling. It’s a Giving Tree thing. Hello? Hello?

EF’s philosophy of beauty in subtraction translates into much of their most important work as gardeners of a $400+ billion ecosystem being accomplished behind the scenes, away from the spotlight. They don’t ask for credit because getting credit could make them appear larger than those they support, which wouldn’t be the best way to foster independent growth.

What many fail to appreciate is that given the recruiting challenges, the EF is a relatively small organization that is even more constrained by attention bottlenecks than its dwindling share of the premine, now less than 0.4% of the ETH supply. When the price of ETH goes up that can seem like a lot of money, but it’s not much compared with the size of the Ethereum ecosystem, especially if we consider how long that might need to last.

Being understaffed and overburdened means working with the EF can feel infuriatingly slow from the outside while internally they’re exhausted from running around trying to do everything. EF deserves more appreciation than it gets. It’s not just the burden of work that is hard, it’s the burden of responsibility. EF people sometimes feel like they’re expected to carry the entire weight of Ethereum on their backs.

This is not only unfair, it’s also unsustainable. How long can 0.4% of the ETH supply last? What happens after? How tragic will be our tragedy of commons? Will the kind of corporations & VCs that embraced and extended the Internet embrace and extend the critical parts we didn’t finish building as public goods? As private solutions merge and consolidate will we be able to resist the creeping force of centralisation? Could we end up like the Internet pioneers that came before us, waking up a decade later to discover our decentralised vision for Ethereum was embraced, extended and then extinguished? Will we welcome our new overlords?

For Ethereum to scale while staying true to its values we have to step up, plant more “giving trees” and encourage our best and brightest to work on public goods by showing how much we appreciate and value those who are already doing their best.

Since it will take time to grow this decentralized forest of giving trees, we should have a sense of urgency and start way before all that’s left from the EF is a sad little stump.

Our pledge to Ethereum values

A pledge is a type of Schelling fence that protects future versions of ourselves from sliding down slippery slopes and losing our values. To be clear, what we mean by values are principles we won’t give up to be more successful. If you’re willing to sacrifice your “values” for gain you don’t have values, you have marketing.

Though we’re not certain of much we are certain enough to pledge the following:

  1. Forever aligned with Ethereum’s values: We pledge to continue developing GSN as a decentralized, permissionless and trust-minimized infrastructure that is aligned with the values of Ethereum.
  2. Forever open source, as defined by the Open Source Initiative: We pledge to never hop this fence. We believe being fork-friendly in this space is a feature, not a bug.

Projects that can’t be forked are all or nothing propositions. The easier it is to unbundle the bad from the good, the harder it is for bad stuff to accumulate.

A fork-friendly project is not only competing with other projects in its category but also implicitly with other possible variations of itself. Competition is an entropy pump. It’s a healthy balance against both honest mistakes and malicious abuses of power. Teams of fork-friendly projects have to rely more on legitimacy, which keeps them more closely aligned with the community. They’re still somewhat shielded from competition by having network effects, technical expertise, branding and momentum on their side. Isn’t that enough?

Accepting the legitimacy of non-open source licenses in the Ethereum ecosystem could have a chilling effect on forks, increase centralization around founding teams, strengthen the regulatory case against developers, and encourage a more litigious ecosystem where having access to regulators and high powered lawyers is a significant source of competitive advantage. Let’s not go there.

Why getting it right took longer than expected

Developing a new system can be a bit like driving at night. It’s hard to see too far ahead, but as you move forward you see far enough into the darkness to avoid hitting walls, and you just keep doing that over and over again until you get all the way home.

When we started developing GSN v2 we suspected not everything would go according to the plan. The future is full of unpredictable games of missing information. We don’t get to choose the cards we’re dealt, only how we play them.

As expected, we did in fact run into some unexpected challenges. For example, it was harder and took longer than we predicted to get multiple high-quality security audits for a non-trivial extension to the Ethereum stack. Also, we didn’t originally anticipate having to optimize GSN so soon for a congested network with rapidly changing gas prices. Oh, and there was the whole global pandemic thing.

In total these ended up significantly increasing the scope and length of our original development roadmap. It was tempting to cut corners than take more time at lower pay to do it right — after all, we could have easily decided, the perfect is the enemy of the good, and software is never “done” anyway. And for typical product development, cutting some corners may well have been the right choice.

But for decentralized infrastructure to have legitimacy it has to be more like a bridge than a house of cards. There’s no centralized entity that can easily coordinate rebuilding it if it breaks. So there’s no excuse for compromising on the dimensions of quality that matter the most. Being able to tell what those more important dimensions of quality are is a skill — easier said than done, but nevertheless a kind of perfection worth striving for.

GSN roadmap & upcoming improvements

Ethereum is still in the early adopter stage. Compared with the world of centralized apps our ecosystem is still tiny. To help catalyze mass adoption and reach the next billion users we will need to solve many hard and interesting problems. At a minimum, we will need dapps that just work, cheaply and at massive scale without requiring users to grapple with new concepts like gas. The less friction the better.

To help Ethereum get there upcoming improvements in GSN will help minimize gas costs, scale with new technologies, and extend the protocol to work for both writing and reading on-chain state in order to provide infrastructure for ultra light clients that can run in the browser and sync trustlessly with the network in seconds from incentivized full nodes that get paid to store and serve state.

Providing decentralized infrastructure for ultra light clients will not only be great for dapps, but also healthier for a network that would otherwise be forced to choose between breaking dapps with state rent or risk having state spiral so out of control that the only full nodes in the network are run by a few big companies.

Behind the scenes the transaction fees needed for all these interactions will be abstracted away. Users will no more have to think about who is paying for gas than they currently think about who is paying for server fees when they interact with a centralized app.

We will be sharing more details soon. If you’re interested in solving hard problems with decentralization please reach out 10X@opengsn.org.
